drug_class: Calcium channel blocker (used specifically for brain blood vessels)
purpose: Nimodipine is used to help prevent brain damage after a certain type of bleeding in the brain called a subarachnoid hemorrhage. It works by keeping the blood vessels in your brain from tightening up too much after the bleed. This helps make sure your brain continues to get enough blood flow during your recovery.
how_it_works: Think of your blood vessels like a garden hose — when they squeeze too tight, not enough blood gets through. Nimodipine blocks calcium from entering the muscle cells of blood vessel walls, which helps those vessels stay relaxed and open. This is especially important in the brain after a bleed, where tight vessels can cause serious damage.
common_side_effects: Low blood pressure (you may feel dizzy or lightheaded), flushing or feeling warm, headache, nausea, slow or fast heartbeat, and swelling in your legs or ankles. Let your doctor or pharmacist know if any of these bother you.
warnings: This medication can lower your blood pressure significantly, so stand up slowly to avoid dizziness and falls. Never crush the capsule and inject the liquid — this has caused serious harm and death. If you have liver problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, since many drugs can interact with nimodipine.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 60 mg (one capsule or oral liquid) taken every 4 hours for 21 days after the brain bleed. It is very important to take it on schedule — even through the night. Your nurse or caregiver may help you keep track while you are in the hospital.
